idiom_name: for msg := range in { if keep(msg) { out <- msg } } / slices.DeleteFunc
implementation_notes: Go has no filter combinator for channels, so the canonical realization is the range loop plus a `func(Msg) bool` closure, with `continue` (or a discard send) as the reject path; for slices the standard library names the operation - `slices.DeleteFunc(s, func(m Msg) bool { return !keep(m) })` filters in place, and `slices.Collect`/`slices.Values` bridge slices and iterators. A MessageFilter type is only justified when the criterion travels as configuration (a closure injected into a consumer struct) or when several criteria compose into a chain.
pitfalls: Filtering inside one consumer of a shared channel removes the message for everyone: when the criterion is per-consumer, filter before delivery (separate queue/subscription) or fan out first.
`continue` hides rejects; without a counter or a discard channel a too-strict predicate looks exactly like an idle system.
A predicate that blocks (network call, mutex) blocks the consumer goroutine and, on a single-consumer queue, back-pressures the producer - resolve the criterion outside the loop or make it cheap.

variants.name: Lazy iterator pipeline (range-over-func)
variants.idiom_name: iter.Seq[Msg] composition with for-range over a function
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.23 added range-over-func and the `iter` package, so a filter becomes a named function over `iter.Seq[T]` - `func Keep(seq iter.Seq[Msg], pred func(Msg) bool) iter.Seq[Msg]` - consumed by an ordinary `for msg := range` loop; filters compose lazily without materialising slices and `slices.Values`/`slices.Collect` bridge slices and iterators. Choose it for pipelines of several stages (filter, transform, aggregate) that would otherwise be nested loops; a plain range loop stays simpler for a single criterion.
pitfalls: A sequence function must stop as soon as yield returns false; ignoring the result breaks `break` in the caller and can iterate forever.
Iterators are single-use: ranging the same iter.Seq twice yields nothing (or replays side effects) - rebuild the pipeline for each pass.
iter.Seq is pull-based and carries no concurrency guarantees; ranging it from several goroutines races on the underlying source.
